title: Arrays
description: One- and multi-dimensional arrays, initialization, traversal, and array bounds.
objectives: Declare, initialize, and traverse one-dimensional arrays
Understand that C performs no automatic bounds checking

content.heading: One-Dimensional Arrays and Bounds
content.body: An array is a fixed-size, contiguous block of same-typed elements: int numbers[5]; declares an uninitialized array of 5 ints; int numbers[] = {1, 2, 3}; declares and initializes one, with its size (3) inferred from the initializer list. Valid indices run from 0 to size - 1. Critically, unlike Java or Python, C performs no automatic bounds checking whatsoever: accessing numbers[10] on a 5-element array does not raise any error — it reads or writes whatever memory happens to be at that (out-of-bounds) location, silently corrupting nearby data or crashing unpredictably. This is a foundational source of C bugs and security vulnerabilities (buffer overflows), and the programmer is entirely responsible for staying within bounds.

content.heading: Multidimensional Arrays and Passing to Functions
content.body:
A two-dimensional array, int grid[3][4];, is laid out in memory as one contiguous block, row by row (row-major order) — grid[i][j] accesses row i, column j. Traversal typically uses nested for loops over both dimensions.

When an array is passed to a function, it decays into a pointer to its first element — the function receives no information about the array's original length (sizeof inside the function would report a pointer's size, not the array's), so the length must always be passed as a separate parameter alongside the array itself: void process(int arr[], int length) { ... }.

content.explanation: sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]) correctly computes the element count only in main(), where numbers is still a true array — this pattern would give a wrong result if written inside printAll(), where arr is really just a pointer.

keyPoints: C performs no automatic bounds checking — out-of-range array access is undefined behavior, not a caught error
Multidimensional arrays are stored contiguously in row-major order
An array passed to a function decays into a pointer, losing its size information
Always pass an array's length as a separate parameter, since sizeof won't work correctly inside the function
commonMistakes: Reading or writing an out-of-bounds array index, silently corrupting memory
Using sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) inside a function that received arr as a parameter, getting a wrong (pointer-based) result
Off-by-one errors in loop bounds against an array's size
